lesson.title: Stamping a Pattern: Multiplying a String by a Number
lesson.summary: String repetition uses the * operator between a string and an integer to build a new string containing the original string repeated that many times.
lesson.body:
Just as + is repurposed for joining strings, Python repurposes * to repeat them. The expression "ab" * 3 does not mean multiplication in the arithmetic sense; it means build a new string by repeating "ab" three times, producing "ababab". The integer tells Python how many copies to lay end to end, and the result is a single new string, since like all string operations this does not modify the original value.

A common practical use is drawing a separator line for printed output. The statement border = "-" * 20 stores a string of twenty dash characters in a row, useful for framing a title or dividing sections of text on the screen. Trace it directly: Python takes the one-character string "-" and repeats it twenty times, so border ends up holding "--------------------", which you could then print above and below a heading.

The order of the operands is flexible: 3 * "ab" produces the exact same result as "ab" * 3, since Python recognizes the pattern regardless of which side the integer is on. What is not flexible is the types involved. Exactly one operand must be a string and the other must be an integer; trying "ab" * "cd", multiplying two strings together, raises a TypeError, because Python has no defined meaning for that combination.

Edge cases are worth tracing carefully. "x" * 0 evaluates to an empty string, "", since repeating something zero times leaves nothing. A negative number behaves the same way as zero, also producing an empty string rather than an error, which surprises some learners who expect a crash. Understanding these edge cases matters because loops or calculations that compute a repeat count sometimes accidentally produce zero or a negative number, and it helps to know the result will be an empty string rather than a program crash.

It helps to see repetition as a shortcut for something you could build with concatenation instead: "ab" * 3 produces the same result as "ab" + "ab" + "ab", but repetition expresses the intent more directly when the number of copies is known and states clearly that the same piece is being repeated rather than several different pieces being joined. Beyond separator lines, repetition is used for indentation (" " * 4 to indent four spaces), simple text-based progress bars ("#" * completed + "-" * remaining), and any situation where a pattern needs to be stamped out a fixed number of times.

Repetition and concatenation frequently work together in the same line. Consider header = "=" * 10 + " Menu " + "=" * 10. Python builds this in pieces: "=" * 10 produces a ten-character string of equal signs, and it appears twice in the expression, once on each side of the literal text " Menu ", which itself is six characters including its leading and trailing spaces. Concatenating all three pieces with + in order produces "========== Menu ==========", a tidy twenty-six character banner built from just two operators and one short literal, a pattern common in text-based menus and reports.
